opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, looking back, I think those early struggles were really valuable, even though at the time they just felt frustrating.

When I first started working on NLP and Transformers, I didn't really know what I was doing. I'd read the papers, I'd try to reproduce results, and things just wouldn't work. The loss would blow up, or the numbers would be way off from what was reported, and I'd spend days or weeks trying to figure out whether it was a bug in my code, a missing trick nobody had written down, or that I'd misunderstood the idea. A lot of the time it was something embarrassingly small, like a learning rate warmup or a normalization detail.

At the time I sometimes felt I wasn't cut out for research, because everyone else seemed to be producing results and I was stuck debugging. But what I eventually realized is that this debugging process is where most of the real learning happens. You build an intuition for what a healthy training run looks like, where things tend to break, and how to isolate problems systematically. That engineering sense ended up being one of the most useful skills I have, much more than any single paper.

The other lesson was about choosing problems. Early on I was chasing directions that were very crowded, where lots of strong groups with far more compute were working on the same thing. It's hard to make a meaningful contribution there as a student. That pushed me to think more carefully about where I could actually add something, which is part of why I gravitated toward infrastructure and tooling, things that make other people's research easier, and later toward reinforcement learning.

So if I could talk to my younger self, I'd say: the struggle isn't a sign you're failing. It's the training process. Just make sure you're learning something transferable from it, and don't be afraid to change direction when you see a better fit for your strengths.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the struggles were valuable and taught transferable skills, but does not suggest they would have happened the same way even if Weng’s present self had helped their past self.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, when I look back at that period, I mostly remember feeling lost. This was around 2017, 2018, when Transformers had just come out, and everyone around me was pivoting to NLP. I was an undergrad at Tsinghua, and I jumped in because it felt like the thing to do, not because I understood it deeply.

I spent months reading papers I only half understood, and the research itself never clicked. I'd try an idea, it wouldn't work, and I couldn't tell whether it was my implementation, my understanding, or the idea itself. There was no feedback loop. That's a brutal way to learn, because you can't tell if you're getting better.

What eventually saved me was realizing I cared much more about the systems side than the modeling side. I liked making things run fast, making code clean, making the whole pipeline actually work end to end. That's what led me into reinforcement learning infrastructure and eventually to building Tianshou. In RL, if your environment loop is slow or buggy, nothing works, so engineering quality mattered in a way I could feel immediately. That was the feedback loop I'd been missing.

So I don't think of those struggles as wasted time. They taught me what I'm not good at, and more importantly, what I actually enjoy. A lot of people in research feel pressure to be the person inventing the new architecture. It took me failing at that to figure out that building the tools everyone else relies on is just as valuable, and for me, a lot more fun.

r001.rationale: The response describes feeling lost and later finding a better fit in systems work, but it does not suggest the struggles would have turned out the same if Weng’s present self had helped his past self.

astra-6.text:
Looking back, I’d describe it as learning to be comfortable with not understanding something right away. With Transformers and NLP, it’s easy to recognize the terminology before you can really explain how the pieces fit together. That gap can be frustrating.

I think the useful response is to make the questions smaller: What do I understand? Where does my explanation break down? What could I try to clarify that? To me, that’s part of learning how to do research—turning confusion into a question you can actually work on.

r001.rationale: The response describes coping with confusion by breaking questions down, but does not suggest that the struggles might have turned out the same even if Weng’s present self had helped her past self.

sol-6.1.text: Looking back, I think the hardest part was learning to be comfortable with not understanding everything right away. With Transformers and NLP, there are so many ideas connected to one another that you can read a paper and still feel like you’re missing something. I had to slow down, revisit the fundamentals, and work through things step by step. That process could be frustrating, but it also taught me patience. I’ve come to see that confusion as part of research—you keep asking questions, and gradually things start to connect.
